title: Episode 41: The Carving of Mount Rushmore: Gutzon Borglum's Colossi

Between 1927 and 1941, passionate and temperamental sculptor Gutzon Borglum led an army of four hundred miners and stonecutters in the Black Hills of South Dakota to carve the colossal faces of Washington, Jefferson, Lincoln, and Roosevelt out of solid granite. Using ninety percent dynamite and breeches buoys hanging hundreds of feet in the air, they created the world's greatest mountain monument without a single fatality.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Rising five thousand seven hundred feet above sea level in the Black Hills of South Dakota stands one of the most recognizable and awe-inspiring monuments in human history: Mount Rushmore. Carved out of an ancient batholith of solid Harney Peak granite, the four sixty-foot-tall faces of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln gaze serenely across the American continent. But behind this monumental triumph of art and engineering was a fourteen-year epic of sheer grit, creative madness, and explosive danger. Directed by the brilliant, temperamental sculptor Gutzon Borglum, four hundred miners and stonecutters blasted four hundred and fifty thousand tons of rock using dynamite, jackhammers, and wire cables suspended hundreds of feet above jagged chasms—achieving the impossible without losing a single human life. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: DOANE ROBINSON'S DREAM AND THE ARRIVAL OF BORGLUM
The vision for Mount Rushmore began in nineteen twenty-three in the fertile imagination of South Dakota state historian Doane Robinson. Seeking an audacious way to draw newly motorized automobile tourists across the dusty dirt highways of the Great Plains to the Black Hills, Robinson proposed carving colossal statues of Western frontier icons—including Meriwether Lewis, William Clark, Buffalo Bill Cody, and Lakota Chief Red Cloud—directly into the granite pinnacles known as the Needles. Robinson reached out to John Gutzon de la Mothe Borglum, a flamboyant, internationally renowned sixty-year-old American sculptor who had studied under master sculptor Auguste Rodin in Paris. Borglum was an eccentric, combative genius of boundless ego and monumental ambition who believed American art should match the vast physical scale of the continent. Borglum looked at Robinson's proposal and instantly rejected carving regional Western figures, declaring with booming conviction: 'American history is too large to carve local heroes. We must carve a national memorial that speaks to the world!' Borglum also rejected the crumbling, narrow Needles, scouting the Black Hills on horseback until he stood before Mount Rushmore—a colossal, pristine mountain of fine-grained Harney Peak granite that soared five thousand seven hundred feet above sea level, bathed in direct southern sunlight from sunrise to sunset. Borglum pointed to the pristine stone and declared: 'America will march along that skyline!' South Dakota state historian Doane Robinson dreamed of carving western heroes like Red Cloud, Lewis and Clark, and Buffalo Bill Cody into the granite spires of the Needles to attract automobile tourists. Local Lakota tribes protested the desecration of the sacred Paha Sapa, regarding the dynamiting of the granite peaks as an unforgivable violation of the Fort Laramie Treaty.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE FOUR FACES OF THE REPUBLIC
Borglum carefully selected four presidents who would symbolize the birth, growth, preservation, and development of the American democratic experiment over its first one hundred and fifty years. George Washington represented the nation's founding, constitutional integrity, and struggle for independence; Thomas Jefferson represented the expansion of the republic through the Louisiana Purchase and the soaring ideals of the Declaration of Independence; Abraham Lincoln represented the preservation of the Union and the abolition of slavery during the crucible of the Civil War; and Theodore Roosevelt—a personal friend and hunting companion of Borglum—represented the modern economic development of the nation, the conservation of national parks, and the construction of the Panama Canal. Borglum created intricate five-foot-tall plaster models of the monument in his studio, scaling them mathematically at a ratio of one to twelve: one inch on the plaster model equaled one foot on the mountain. To transfer the three-dimensional measurements from the model to the granite precipice, Borglum designed an ingenious pointing machine: a thirty-foot rotating steel boom mounted on the top of the mountain with a protractor, plumb bob, and weighted cables that allowed stonecutters to mark precise drill depths across thousands of coordinate points on the cliff face. Borglum insisted that the monument must represent the birth, growth, preservation, and development of the American republic, selecting Washington, Jefferson, Lincoln, and Theodore Roosevelt as the colossal quartet. Borglum surveyed the cliffs from horseback, marveling at the towering granite faces that caught the morning light above the whispering ponderosa pines.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: SCULPTING WITH DYNAMITE
Carving four sixty-foot heads out of a natural mountain required moving four hundred and fifty thousand tons of solid granite. Hand-chiseling was physically impossible; Borglum turned to an unconventional sculpting tool: dynamite. Over ninety percent of the rock removed from Mount Rushmore was blasted away by high explosives. Borglum hired a crew of four hundred local men—predominantly out-of-work Black Hills gold miners, lumberjacks, and stonecutters—who were skilled in drilling and explosives. Every morning, workers climbed seven hundred steep wooden steps up the mountain before strapping themselves into heavy leather harness swings called 'breeches buoys' attached to three-eighths-inch steel cables, dangling hundreds of feet above the steep abyss. Master powder men drilled deep blast holes with pneumatic jackhammers, loaded them with carefully calibrated fractional sticks of dynamite, lit fuses, and signaled to be winched up the cliff face just before the mountain erupted in a deafening thunder of flying granite. The powder men achieved astonishing precision: blasting away rock to within just three inches of the final facial contour without cracking the delicate granite beneath. Over ninety percent of the four hundred and fifty thousand tons of granite was removed using precisely calculated micro-charges of dynamite, blasted by miners hanging in bosun chairs suspended by steel cables five hundred feet above the valley floor.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE JEFFERSON DISASTER AND THE SHIFTING MOUNTAIN
Working on a natural mountain brought heart-stopping geological surprises. Borglum originally designed Thomas Jefferson to sit to the right of George Washington. In nineteen thirty-four, after months of drilling and blasting, Jefferson's face was nearly half-completed when miners hit a deep, catastrophic fault line: a fissure of soft, crumbly feldspar that compromised the entire right side of the mountain. Fearing that Jefferson's nose and forehead would collapse in the first frost, Borglum made an audacious, agonizing decision: he ordered the entire half-carved face of Thomas Jefferson to be blasted off the mountain with dynamite, reducing months of painstaking work to rubble in seconds. Borglum then redesigned the composition, moving Jefferson to the left of Washington, wedged between Washington and Lincoln. The engineering recalculation required re-surveying the entire cliff face, but Borglum's artistic adaptability triumphed over the flawed stone. When a flawed vein of feldspar cracked across Jefferson face on Washington right side, Borglum blasted the unfinished carving off the mountain with dynamite and re-carved Jefferson on Washington left.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: HONEYCOMBING AND THE BUMPER FINISH
Once the dynamite blasted the granite to within three inches of the final surface, workers transitioned to delicate hand-finishing techniques. Using heavy pneumatic jackhammers, miners drilled hundreds of closely spaced holes side by side in a dense grid pattern known as 'honeycombing.' Workers then broke off the remaining stone pegs with small steel wedges and sledgehammers. Finally, the surface was smoothed using a pneumatic tool called a 'bumper'—a micro-chisel fitted with four sharp steel points that pulverized the rough granite surface, leaving behind a smooth, polished texture as refined as an indoor marble statue. Workers dangled in their swings for eight hours a day in freezing sub-zero mountain winds and blistering ninety-degree summer heat, their hands calloused, their ears deafened by the roar of air compressors. Borglum personally inspected every inch of the carving, communicating through megaphones from the valley floor and sending telephone corrections to his son, Lincoln Borglum, who served as the on-mountain construction superintendent. Borglum used pneumatic bumper drills to smooth the rough granite until the sixty-foot presidential faces acquired the luminous finish of ancient marble statues under the midday sun.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SECRET HALL OF RECORDS
Borglum envisioned Mount Rushmore not merely as a sculpture, but as a time capsule for future civilizations thousands of years in the future. Deep into the solid granite wall of the canyon behind the four heads, Borglum began blasting out a massive seventy-foot-deep chamber known as the 'Hall of Records.' Borglum planned an immense arched cavern with bronze doors, featuring display cases containing the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and bronze plaques detailing the history of the United States, so that future archaeologists who discovered the monument would understand who carved it and why. Although federal funding cuts during the Great Depression and the threat of World War Two halted construction of the Hall before it could be completed, in nineteen ninety-eight, Borglum's vision was finally fulfilled: a teakwood box containing sixteen porcelain enamel panels inscribed with the history of the monument was permanently sealed in a titanium vault inside the floor of the canyon entry. Behind the stone hairline of Lincoln, Borglum excavated an eighty-foot Hall of Records, intended to preserve parchment copies of the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution for future civilizations.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: COMPLETION AND THE ZERO-FATALITY MIRACLE
In March nineteen forty-one, with the monument nearing completion, seventy-three-year-old Gutzon Borglum passed away in Chicago following complications from surgery. His devoted son, Lincoln Borglum, took over the leadership, guiding the crew through the final carving of Lincoln's eyes and Washington's collar. On October thirty-first, nineteen forty-one, with America on the brink of entering World War Two, work on Mount Rushmore was officially declared complete. In fourteen years of hair-raising high-altitude construction—handling hundreds of tons of dynamite and dangling hundreds of feet in the air on thin wire cables—not a single worker lost his life, establishing an unprecedented safety miracle in monumental engineering. Today, Mount Rushmore welcomes more than three million visitors annually. Standing before the colossal granite faces carved into the mountain sky, visitors marvel at the audacity of an eccentric sculptor and the extraordinary courage of American miners who turned a mountain into an eternal sanctuary of human freedom.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Mount Rushmore is an extraordinary testament to the marriage of fine art and heavy engineering. It proves that with vision, courage, and perseverance, even the granite bones of the earth can be sculpted into enduring monuments to the human spirit. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we head to Nebraska for the wild saga of Buffalo Bill Cody and his Wild West show. Until then, stay curious.
